newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia seeks to avoid contentious issues with Europe.
newsitem.headline: Asia seeks to avoid contentious issues with Europe.

text.p: ASEAN members and other Asian countries want to avoid contentious political issues and focus on economic cooperation at meetings with European nations later this month, regional analysts and government sources say.
But whether or not Europe will cooperate remains to be seen.
"ASEAN's agenda for the 12th ASEAN-EU Ministerial Meeting is to focus on economic and other cooperation issues," said Yeo Lay Hwee of Singapore's state-linked Institute of Policy Studies.

She said ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) would want to take up a proposal by the EU Commission, the EU's executive arm, that the 1980 ASEAN-EU Cooperation Agreement be replaced by an Action Plan containing concrete initiatives in development cooperation.

Japanese and Thai foreign ministry officials said contentious issues such as Burma's human rights record, Indonesia's military occupation of East Timor, human rights and labour standards should not dominate the meetings.
Ministers from ASEAN, which groups Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam, will meet their EU counterparts in Singapore on February 13-14.
This will be followed by the first Asia-Europe Foreign Ministers (ASEM) meeting on February 15, involving ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea and the 15-nation EU.

Analysts said Asia's agenda at the ASEM meeting will follow up on economic and political deals made at its inaugural summit in Bangkok last March, with the launch of the Asia-Europe Foundation and the Greater Mekong project topping the list.

The latter is a comprehensive infrastructure development plan in areas through which the Mekong River flows--Cambodia, Laos, Burma, Thailand, Vietnam and southern China's Yunnan province. The Asia-Europe Foundation seeks to promote cultural exchanges.
Diplomats also said the foreign ministers would need to set an agenda for next year's Asia-Europe summit in London.

One topic likely to emerge is whether ASEM should expand, an Asian diplomat in Kuala Lumpur said. Australia and India are keen to join but Malaysia, which is pushing its own proposal for an East Asian Economic Caucus (EAEC), has been unenthusiastic.

Japan sees ASEM as important in efforts to construct a post-Cold War international order. "Up until now, Europe-Asia links have been much weaker than U.S-Asia or U.S.-Europe ties," a Japanese official said.
The EU has become ASEAN's third biggest trade partner with more than $85 billion in goods and services changing hands in 1994-1995.
A Filipino official said ASEAN is expected to present a common front if the EU raised political issues such as East Timor and Burma, which could result in a stalemate in the talks.
Such issues could be raised informally, he said. "If they raise them in a non-confrontational way, which does not smack of interference in ASEAN affairs, that would be all right."

Last July, the European Commission told ASEAN to stop coddling Burma's military junta as it might upset relations with Europe. ASEAN retaliated by threatening to drop the EU from the annual ASEAN Regional Forum.
But analysts said while the EU and ASEAN may never agree on Burma or East Timor, trade relations have flourished.

Nevertheless, Yeo said ASEAN-EU relations might suffer with Burma's entrance into the regional grouping, which ASEAN has said would happen at the same time as that of Laos and Cambodia. Some say this could happen as early as this year to coincide with ASEAN's 30th anniversary.
"EU as a matter of principle would find it difficult to agree on any cooperation projects that would involve Burma."
Yeo said since the EU would object to Burma's participation in ASEM, it would increasingly rely on the ASEM channel to get things going in this region, hence downgrading ties with ASEAN.
"This is especially so if the ASEM gathers more momentum as some of the flagship projects suggested during the first ASEM leaders meeting (take) off smoothly and start to see some results," she said.

Analysts also said economic cooperation may not be particularly smooth in the future. Some EU members believe that calls by ASEAN, particularly Singapore, for more economic development imply that Europeans will provide just the financing and Asians the expertise.

Yeo said this is a very narrow view of cooperation as the private sector has been actively encouraged to take part in various projects which "do represent some opportunities for some EU businesses to gain a foothold in this region."
The EU is also expected to push for a "Multi-lateral Investment Agreement" at the ASEM meeting, diplomats said.

The pact, under negotiation at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, calls for a level playing field between foreign and domestic investors, more transparency in awarding government contracts and international labour standards, including a ban on child labour.
The pact is generally opposed by Asian countries, which say it would give an unfair advantage to more-developed economies.
